lines.text: Centuries ago, my little readers might expect a king, but this story begins with a common block of firewood.
Somehow, that unremarkable log found its way into the workshop of Mastro Cherry, an old carpenter with a round, red nose.
Seeing the sturdy piece of wood, he happily decided it had arrived just in time to become the leg of a table.
Yet, as he raised his hatchet for the first blow, a faint voice pleaded with him not to strike so hard.
Astonished, Mastro Cherry searched beneath the bench, inside the closet, and among the shavings, but discovered no one.
Embarrassed by his fear, he convinced himself that the mysterious voice had existed only in his imagination.
No sooner had he struck the wood than the distant little voice cried out that he had hurt it.
Mastro Cherry stood speechless, with his eyes bulging and his mouth hanging open in disbelief.
Trembling, he wondered whether an ordinary piece of firewood had somehow learned to weep like a child.
Determined to uncover the trick, he seized the log and knocked it against the floor, the walls, and even the ceiling.
After waiting in silence, he forced a laugh and once again blamed his imagination.
Hoping to recover his courage, the terrified carpenter began to sing while he worked.
But when he moved the plane across the wood, the hidden voice giggled and complained that its stomach was being tickled.
At that, poor Mastro Cherry collapsed as though he had been struck, and awoke sitting helplessly on the floor.
